entries.narration: Let's start with the application we will follow through the whole course: a small online shop. A shopper opens the page for product p one thousand and one. The browser asks Route fifty three, the D N S service, for the shop's address, then sends an H T T P S request to a load balancer. The load balancer passes it to one of our app servers, which reads the product from the orders database and links to its image in object storage. Three ideas sit inside that picture. First, every one of those resources is on demand. We create it with an A P I call, and we pay while it exists, not for a machine we bought. Second, some of them are managed services. We never patch the load balancer, and A W S runs the database engine; we only configure them. Third, elasticity. Look at the chart. One app server handles a hundred and fifty requests a second. Overnight, demand is sixty. During the day it is two hundred and forty, and on a sale evening it reaches five hundred and sixty. If we size for the peak, we run four servers all day, which is ninety six server hours. If capacity follows demand, we run one server for eight hours, two for ten, and four for six, which is fifty two server hours, about forty six percent fewer. Now the misconception. The cloud does not scale by itself. You write the scaling rules, a new server takes minutes to be ready, so the evening rise must be anticipated, and account quotas put a ceiling on how many you can start. So the operating model changes who buys hardware, but you still own the design, the configuration, and the bill.

Every A W S service splits the work between two owners, and the split is worth knowing before anything goes wrong. A W S is responsible for security of the cloud: the buildings, the hardware, the host operating systems, and the virtualisation layer that runs your instances. You are responsible for security in the cloud: how you configure things, the code you deploy, who you let in, and your data. The important part is that the line moves with the service. Read the matrix for our ordering app. Our app servers run on E C two, which is infrastructure as a service, so we patch the guest operating system, we install the software, and we set the network rules around each instance. The database runs on R D S. There, A W S patches the operating system and the database engine, but it does so in a maintenance window we choose, and the tables and S Q L are still ours. A Lambda function goes further: A W S runs the runtime, and we own the code and its permissions. S three has no servers for us at all. Yet look at the bottom two rows. Who may access the data, and how it is backed up, are ours for every service on the board. The list on the right turns this into incidents. An unpatched operating system on an app server is our problem. A bucket policy that allows public reads is our problem. A failed disk under the database host is A W S's problem. The misconception to avoid is that managed means secure. A managed service runs correctly, but it does exactly what you configured it to do. So the summary is simple: access and data are always yours, and everything else depends on the service you chose.

Every resource you create lives somewhere, and where it lives decides what can take it down. A Region is a geographic area with its own copy of the services and its own endpoints. Our shop runs in E U west two, which is London. Inside a Region are Availability Zones, groups of data centres with separate power, cooling and networking, close enough for fast links but far enough apart that one local failure should not reach the others. E U west two has three. One small trap: the names A, B and C can point at different physical zones in different accounts in some Regions, so when accounts must agree, they compare zone I Ds instead. Now place the parts of our app. An app server is zonal; it lives in exactly one zone. An S three bucket is Regional; A W S spreads it across zones for us. Our single orders database is placed in one zone, which matters later. And some services are global, outside any one Region: I A M, Route fifty three, and CloudFront. Now the arithmetic. At the evening peak we need four app servers. If we run one per zone, that is three, which is already short, and if a zone fails only two remain. If we run two per zone, that is six. Lose a zone and four remain, which carries the peak. Those two extra servers are the price of surviving a zone failure, and you pay it every hour. The misconception is that multi A Z makes you unstoppable. A Region-wide problem, a bad deployment, or deleted data reaches every zone at once. So decide which boundary you must survive, and pay for exactly the spare capacity that survival needs.

Before we create anything, we need a safe way in. An A W S account is a container: it holds resources, it receives one bill, and it draws a boundary around permissions. Every account has a root user, the email address that created it, and the root user can do everything, including closing the account. So we protect it with multi factor authentication, which A W S now enforces for root users, and we use it only for the handful of tasks that truly need it. Organizations can go further and remove root credentials from member accounts entirely. Daily work happens through I A M Identity Center instead. Follow alex, a developer joining the shop's development account. On the left is alex's configuration. It names the sign-in portal, the account, four four four four, five five five five, six six six six, and the role called ShopDeveloper. Running a w s s s o login opens a browser, where alex enters a password and an M F A code. Then a w s s t s get caller identity asks the Security Token Service a simple question: who am I? Look at the answer. The A R N says assumed role. Alex is not a user with a stored key; alex is holding temporary credentials for a role, and by default that role session lasts one hour, configurable up to twelve, before it must be renewed. The misconception is that an access key in a file is simpler. It is simpler, until it leaks. A long-term key never expires, and it works for whoever finds it. Temporary credentials expire on their own. So the pattern is: root locked away, and people working through one sign-in that hands out short sessions.

Whether you click in the console, type in the C L I, or call an S D K from code, the same thing happens underneath: a signed H T T P S request to an A W S service A P I. Learn to read one, and you can read them all. Take this command. It asks S three, using head object, whether the product file for p one thousand and one exists, and for its metadata, without downloading the body. Read it in three parts. Who: the shop dev profile, which supplies the temporary credentials from our last section. Where: the Region, E U west two, which selects the London endpoint. What: one key in one bucket. Now follow the list. The C L I finds the credentials for the profile. It signs the request with Signature Version four, which binds the signature to the key, the Region and the service. The request travels over H T T P S to the Regional S three endpoint. There, I A M checks whether this identity is allowed the action s three get object on that object's A R N. Head object needs the same permission as reading the object. If it is allowed, we get two hundred O K with headers only: one thousand eight hundred and thirty four bytes, J S O N, and encrypted at rest, which S three does by default for new objects. Notice the A R N shapes on the right. An A R N names a resource exactly, but not every A R N carries every field. S three bucket names are global, so their A R Ns have no Region and no account. I A M is global, so its A R Ns have no Region. A DynamoDB table carries both. The misconception is that the console is a separate system. It calls the same A P Is, under the same permission checks. So every call reduces to identity, Region, resource and action, and the answer is a response or an error that tells you which of the four went wrong.

The last foundation is money, because in the cloud every resource you create is a charge until you delete it. The core rule is that charges follow what exists, not only what is running. Look at the ledger for the shop's development environment. The rates here are hypothetical, chosen to make the arithmetic clear, so check the current pricing pages before you rely on any number. With seven hundred and thirty hours in a month, the running environment costs thirty six dollars and twenty one cents. Now stop the app instance. The compute charge, twenty nine dollars twenty, disappears. But seven dollars and one cent remains, because the thirty gigabyte volume still exists, the Elastic I P is still reserved, the snapshot is still stored, and the product images are still in S three. Stopping is not deleting. To see costs by purpose, we tag resources: project equals shop, environment equals dev, owner equals alex. A tag only appears in cost reports once it is activated as a cost allocation tag, so do that early. Then a budget. Set one for the account, with an alert when actual spending passes eighty percent, and another when the forecast passes one hundred. Here is the misconception. A budget is not a spending cap. Budget data is updated up to three times a day, so an alert can arrive after the money is spent. Budget actions can apply a restrictive policy or stop specific E C two or R D S instances, but they only touch what you configured, and charges like storage keep accruing. So: tag on creation, alert early, and delete what you no longer need. With safe access, a request path, and a ledger, we are ready to make identities and permissions explicit, which is the next chapter.
